items.claim: The span's own closing verse carries a rare divine-title formula that the row's closing note denies rather than discloses, leaving the row's end boundary unexplained by what the bytes actually show there.
items.evidence: Jer.50.25 reads כִּי מְלָאכָ֣ה הִ֗יא לַֽאדֹנָ֧י יְהוִ֛ה צְבָא֖וֹת בְּאֶ֥רֶץ כַּשְׂדִּֽים (byte tier) -- a prefixed la-adonai plus YHWH-tsevaot title stack, occurring at exactly two sites in the book, both in the Babylon-nations-oracle block (sweep: 2 verses -- Jer.46.10, Jer.50.25). The row's own span ends on this verse, yet its closing note states the clause 'is not cited here as carrying a divine-title stack' and defers the question elsewhere instead of naming what the bytes plainly carry at the row's own seam. A byte-true formula sitting at a row's own boundary needs disclosure, not denial; as written the row gives no positive account of what closes its own span.

items.claim: The opening imperative and the closing hoy are both read correctly against the book's own formula classes, and both boundaries match the disclosed parashah marks.
items.evidence: The row opens on a discourse-frame imperative series at Jer.50.26 (“Come against her from the farthest border. Open her storehouses.”, verbatim against the staged text) and closes at Jer.50.27, where the setumah inventory (single-witness) matches the row's own disclosure. The hoy inside Jer.50.27 follows a kill-the-bulls command in the same verse and is read as capping that battle call rather than as a fresh woe-onset or funeral cry -- the reading the book's own hoy-role classification assigns to this specific site, distinct from its woe-oracle-onset, day-alas, and funeral-cry uses elsewhere.

items.claim: The row misattributes a comparandum verse to the wrong nation's oracle, naming Ammon for a formula that belongs to the Damascus unit.
items.evidence: Jer.49.26, cited as parallel closing material, falls after the Damascus header at Jer.49.23 and before the next header at Jer.49.28, and sits inside the Damascus unit that itself closes at Jer.49.27 -- not inside the separately headed Ammon unit, which opens at Jer.49.1 and closes at Jer.49.6 without this formula appearing in it at all. The row's own boundary argument (the subject shift to the fleeing refugees, the renewed archers' summons, and the setumah close at Jer.50.30) does not depend on this comparison and stands on its own, but the nation named for the comparandum is wrong as written.

items.claim: The challenge-formula opening and the closing divine-title stack both check out against the book's own inventory, with accurate marks on both boundaries.
items.evidence: Jer.50.31 opens with a direct second-person address (“Behold, I am against you, you proud one”), a stronger seam signal than the third-person material on either side of it, and closes the same verse with a neum-adonai-YHWH-tsevaot title stack -- one of only four such stack sites in the book, alongside Jer.2.19, Jer.2.22, and Jer.49.5 (sweep: 4 verses). The front seam (the setumah at Jer.50.30) and the row's own close (the setumah at Jer.50.32) both match the disclosed inventory, and the quoted clauses are verbatim against the staged text.

items.claim: A quoted clause departs from the staged text's own capitalization, breaking verbatim quotation.
items.evidence: The row quotes the clause closing Jer.50.34 as “he will thoroughly plead their cause”, but the staged text reads “He will thoroughly plead their cause” -- a new sentence following “his name.” rather than a lower-case continuation. The koh-amar-tsevaot onset driving the row's own opening at Jer.50.33, the setumah front seam at Jer.50.32, and the decision not to classify this row as trial_speech despite the shared lawsuit root are otherwise well grounded; the defect is confined to this one quoted clause.

items.claim: The row opens a fresh unit at a verse carrying none of this block's licensed internal-cut signals, and its rejected alternative never engages the stronger rival of one continuous declaration.
items.evidence: Jer.50.35 carries no koh-amar onset and no hoy, and its own grammar is third-person description (“and on the inhabitants of Babylon, on her princes, and on her wise men”) rather than the direct address that opens the row before it (“you proud one” at Jer.50.31). The row's own alternative-reading discussion considers only whether to split the drought line at Jer.50.38 from the sword litany before it; it never considers or rebuts reading the koh-amar-tsevaot declaration opening at Jer.50.33 straight through the litany as one continuous unit, leaving the stronger rival unaddressed.

items.claim: The therefore-clause pivot is argued against its strongest rival rather than a strawman, and the triple-occurrence refrain claim is byte-verified and properly scope-limited.
items.evidence: The row's own alternative-reading discussion explicitly considers and answers the reading that would fold this span into the sword-and-drought litany before it as one unit, naming the pivot at Jer.50.39 as its warrant. The closing clause at Jer.50.40 is byte-identical to the clause closing Jer.49.18 and Jer.49.33 (sweep: 3 verses), and the row limits its claim to those three sites rather than asserting exclusivity book-wide. The heuristic flag on this row's use of 'single' in its alternative-reading sentence describes the rejected reading's shape rather than asserting an exclusivity claim, and is confirmed here as a heuristic artifact, not a real defect.
